result.summary: Pausanias lists the plunderers of the Delphic temple, then traces the history of the Pythian games: the early hymn contest, the addition of harping, pipes, athletic and horse events, and the crown of laurel.

scenes.title: Plunderers of Delphi
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists those who robbed the temple, ending with Nero's removal of 500 bronze statues.
scenes.stakes: The god's treasures at Delphi are repeatedly looted.

scenes.title: Earliest Pythian music contest
scenes.summary: The first contest was a hymn to Apollo; early victors are named, and famous poets like Orpheus, Hesiod and Homer did not compete.

scenes.title: Growth of the Pythian games
scenes.summary: The Amphictyones add pipes, athletics, chariot and horse races; pipe-singing is dropped as gloomy, and the laurel crown is explained by Apollo's love of Daphne.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias explains the laurel crown through Apollo's love of Daphne.

analysis.text: Pausanias links Delphi's sanctity to its history of violation and to the gradual shaping of its festival.
The list of events and Pythiads shows how the games were reorganised from a musical to a mixed athletic festival, with a crown replacing money prizes.

legacy.text: The laurel wreath of the Pythian victors became a lasting symbol of honour, as in 'poet laureate'.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates events by Olympiads and Pythiads, the Greek systems of reckoning time by festival cycles.

language_notes.text: The Eubœan robber, the Phlegyans, Pyrrhus, Xerxes' troops, the Phocians and the Galati (Gauls) are earlier raiders of Delphi, known from other parts of Pausanias.
Purifying Apollo refers to the myth that Apollo needed cleansing after killing the Python at Delphi; Carmanor is said to have done this.
The 48th Olympiad is dated by Olympic reckoning; the Amphictyones are the league of neighbouring states that administered Delphi. Harping means playing the harp (kithara).
The long course and double course are footraces: the long course was many lengths of the stadium, the double course (diaulos) was two lengths.
A Pythiad is the four-year period between Pythian festivals, used for dating. A contest for a crown only means no money prizes were given.
The pancratium was a brutal combination of wrestling and boxing.
The Ptolemies were the Greek kings of Egypt, descended from Alexander's Macedonian general, hence proud of being Macedonians.

context_notes.text: Nero, Roman emperor (reigned AD 54–68), visited Greece in 66–67 and notoriously looted many statues from Delphi.
Orpheus was the legendary singer tied to mystic rites; Musæus was a legendary poet and disciple associated with him.
Clisthenes of Sicyon was an early sixth-century BC tyrant, victorious in the chariot race, and an ally in the Sacred War against Cirrha.

literary_notes.text: Nero, a self-styled artist, is said to despise everything; his theft from the god of the arts is bitterly ironic.
Homer's blindness is treated practically, making him an exceptional figure for whom the harp would be useless.
The laurel crown points back to the myth of Daphne, turning a mythic love story into an explanation of ritual.
